point: A function that cannot serve a call refuses it with raise, which stops the function and hands an Exception with a message to the caller.
why_critical: Slide 7 gives it an idea, a reason and a picture; slide 8 shows three raise checks in box_print; slide 59 and the summary on slide 61 repeat it.

point: An exception is an object with a class, args and a message, and an except clause catches by class, so except Exception also catches a ValueError.
why_critical: Slides 9 and 10 spend two slides on it and the speaker note of slide 9 asks which clause catches both a KeyError and a ValueError.

point: An exception nobody claims climbs from function to caller until a try claims it, and the traceback lists the calls it passed, outermost first.
why_critical: Slides 11 and 12 teach it with the muddy-footprints picture and the closing line, and slide 61 repeats that the traceback shows the way.

point: add_note attaches context to an exception, a bare raise sends the same error on, and the notes are kept in __notes__.
why_critical: Slides 13 and 14 teach it, slide 60 lists it as newer than the book, and the speaker note of slide 13 says a bare raise keeps the original error.

point: Errors of the user are raised; errors of the programmer are asserted.
why_critical: Slide 15 puts it in the part opener, slides 19 and 20 teach it in code, slide 59 closes with raise for the user and assert for the programmer, and practice question 2 on slide 62 asks it.

point: assert states what must be true; it is silent while it holds and raises AssertionError when it fails.
why_critical: Slides 17 and 18 teach it with a sorted list, and the summary on slide 61 repeats it as sentence 2.

point: Python run with -O removes every assert statement, so an assert must never be the only guard of something the program really needs.
why_critical: Slide 21 gives it a title, slide 22 shows it by running the same text twice, the part opener of slide 15 and the summary of slide 61 repeat it, and the speaker note of slide 21 uses a password check.

point: The text after the comma of an assert becomes the message of the AssertionError and is built only when the check fails; without it the message is empty.
why_critical: Slide 19 states it as its idea, slide 20 shows the message in a result row, and slide 18 prints the empty message.

point: Logging levels are names with numbers: DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40 and CRITICAL 50, and a higher number is more serious.
why_critical: Slide 27 gives it a title and a table of five steps, slide 28 prints the five numbers, and the speaker note of slide 26 asks which level a missing file needs.

point: basicConfig is called once; its level argument is the threshold, so messages below it are dropped and the logging calls stay in the code.
why_critical: Slide 29 gives it an idea and a reason, slide 30 runs five calls and shows four lines, and practice question 3 on slide 62 asks which basicConfig arguments decide.

point: A format string such as %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s names the fields of one log line: the time, the level and the text.
why_critical: Slides 31 and 32 teach it with a printed-form picture and a hand-built record.

point: filename= in basicConfig sends the log to a text file instead of the screen, so the evidence stays after the program has ended.
why_critical: Slides 33 and 34 teach it, the part opener of slide 23 names it, and practice question 3 on slide 62 asks it.

point: logging.disable(level) silences that level and every level below it without deleting a logging call, and disable(logging.NOTSET) switches all logging on again.
why_critical: Slides 35 and 36 teach it with a mute-button picture, the part opener of slide 23 names it, and practice question 4 on slide 62 asks it.

point: A logging call with arguments builds its text only if the message is written, while an f-string builds the text first even when nobody reads it.
why_critical: Slides 37 and 38 give it a baker picture and count the calls of __str__ for both styles.

point: A bug is found by reading evidence: with the level at DEBUG the log shows i and total at every step, and factorial(3) prints 0 because range(n + 1) starts the loop at 0.
why_critical: Slides 41 and 42 spend two slides on it, practice question 1 on slide 62 asks it, and the part opener of slide 39 names it as off by one.

point: The fix is range(1, n + 1), and the same log that found the bug proves the fix because the product now grows 1, 2, 6.
why_critical: Slides 43 and 44 are given to the fix, and the speaker note of slide 43 asks why the same log is run again instead of trusting the result.

point: input() always returns text and + joins text, so the answers 5, 3 and 42 make 5342; convert each with int() before adding to get 50.
why_critical: Slides 45 and 46 teach it with the number-cards picture, the closing line repeats it, and the part opener of slide 39 names it as text, not number.

point: A number never equals a text, so toss == guess is false for every guess; the test against the tuple only checks the spelling.
why_critical: Slides 47 and 48 teach it with an apple-and-the-word-apple picture and both repeat the closing line.

point: The fix compares like with like by turning the number into its word first; over 1000 games the buggy comparison wins 0 and the fixed one about half.
why_critical: Slides 49 and 50 teach it and the speaker note of slide 49 asks why a thousand games are used.

point: Step In enters the function a line calls, Step Over runs the line as a whole, Step Out runs the rest of the function, Continue runs to the next breakpoint and Stop ends the program.
why_critical: Slides 53 and 54 are given to the five controls, and the closing line of slide 54 says Step In enters, Step Over skips, Step Out leaves.

point: breakpoint() calls sys.breakpointhook, which normally starts pdb, and setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0 switches every such call off.
why_critical: Slides 57 and 58 teach it, and the speaker note of slide 57 asks how to switch every breakpoint off at once.

point: Choose the instrument by the question: raise for what the caller can fix, assert for what must always be true, logging for what happened, the debugger for the state at one line.
why_critical: Slide 59 is a summary slide with a table and a closing line; slide 3 poses it as the first question of the chapter and slide 62 asks the student to say which instrument was used.

point: The speaker note of the first slide says the chapter teaches four instruments: raise, assert, logging and the debugger.
why_critical: The note of slide 1 names them, and the notes of slides 3 and 59 return to them.

point: An assert with its condition and message in one pair of parentheses, assert (False, 'msg'), tests a tuple and can never fail.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of the assert statement, and the chapter's assert slides use the form without parentheses.
place: The statement assert (False, 'msg') tests a tuple with two items

point: Never catch AssertionError to keep a program going; a check on outside input is an if that raises ValueError.
why_critical: The corpus says it in its watch-out, and the speaker note of slide 18 asks why a real program usually does not catch it.
place: Never catch AssertionError to keep a program going

point: An assertion is not used for a user error because assertions can be removed from a running program.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of choosing an instrument and of argument validation, and slide 21 and its note teach the -O effect.
place: Do not use an assertion for a user error, because assertions can be removed

point: A passing run is not proof of correctness, because a logic error can hide for as long as the test inputs do not touch it.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of the logic error, which the chapter shows twice, in the factorial and in the adding program.
place: A logic error can hide for as long as the test inputs happen not to touch it

point: A logic error runs to the end without any exception and prints a wrong result, so only a person who knows the right answer notices it.
why_critical: The corpus defines it with the adding program, which prints The sum is 5342 without crashing; slides 45 and 46 teach the same program.
place: A logic error is a mistake in the reasoning of a program that lets it run to the end without raising any exception

point: Reading a traceback from the top and stopping at the first entry is a common mistake; the last entry shows where the problem happened.
why_critical: The corpus names it a common mistake in its watch-out of traceback reading, and slides 11 and 12 teach the traceback.
place: Reading from the top and stopping at the first entry is a common mistake

point: Catching Exception hides the difference between a mistake by the user and a mistake by the programmer, so prefer the narrowest class that fits.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of the exception class, and slide 9 teaches that a broad clause catches the more specific class too.
place: Catching Exception is the broadest ordinary choice and hides the difference between a mistake by the user

point: Change one thing at a time and run the program again after each change, so you can tell which change mattered.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of debugging itself.
place: Change one thing at a time, and run the program again after each change

point: After a first implicit logging call such as logging.warning, a later basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is silently ignored and debug lines stay missing.
why_critical: The corpus names it the trap of the default level and of basicConfig, and slide 30 sets the level with force=True because of it.
place: The side effect on the root logger is the trap: after the first implicit call the root logger has a handler

point: To go back after logging.disable, call logging.disable(logging.NOTSET); logging.enable does not exist.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of disabling, and slide 36 shows NOTSET.
place: logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) is the way back, not logging.enable, which does not exist

point: Lazy formatting defers only the formatting; the arguments are still evaluated before the call.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of lazy formatting, and slides 37 and 38 teach the saving.
place: Lazy formatting defers only the formatting. The arguments themselves are evaluated before the call

point: Writing range(n + 1) forgets that range starts at 0, so the first factor is 0 and the whole product is 0, with no error message.
why_critical: The built chapter document explains the off-by-one case at length, and slides 41 and 42 teach it.
place: A programmer who writes range(n + 1) has remembered that the last number is left out and added 1

point: The accumulator of a total must start at the right value and must not be set inside the loop, which resets it on every pass.
why_critical: The corpus names both traps in the watch-out of the accumulator start, a worked case of the chapter.
place: Another trap is to initialise the accumulator inside the loop, which resets it on every pass

point: guess in ('heads') without the comma tests for a substring, and guess == 'heads' or 'tails' is true for every guess.
why_critical: The corpus gives both as the traps of the membership test, one of the six worked cases built on the coin-toss program of slides 47 to 50.
place: With guess in ('heads') the test asks whether guess is a substring of the word heads

point: The six worked cases are small mistakes, most of which print no error message at all and are therefore logic errors.
why_critical: The built chapter document introduces them as the chapter's common mistakes: off-by-one range, accumulator start, string concatenation, random integer, membership test and type mismatch.
place: The worked cases are six small mistakes, each taken from one of the programs of the chapter.

point: Step Over hides what happens inside a call, including a bug, and Step In on the line that calls print() leads into code that does not matter.
why_critical: The corpus gives both warnings, and slide 54 teaches the controls.
place: Step Over hides what happens inside the call, including a bug

point: A breakpoint() left in a program stops it for whoever runs it, so remove it before sharing or set PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of the breakpoint function, and slide 58 teaches the switch.
place: breakpoint() that is left in the program will stop it for whoever runs it

point: The debugger shows only the values the program has at the moment of the pause, not how they got there.
why_critical: The corpus gives it as the watch-out of the debugger, state and inspector pane.
place: The debugger shows only the values that the program has at the moment it is paused

point: The first actual bug was a moth found on 9 September 1947 in relay 70 of the Harvard Mark II and taped into the logbook.
why_critical: The story file states the lesson and slide 6 tells it with the logbook photograph; the speaker note warns that a common file title wrongly says 1945.
place: Debugging has meant removing the moth ever since

point: Brian Kernighan wrote in 1979 that the most effective debugging tool is careful thought with judiciously placed print statements, and logging is the print statement that grew up.
why_critical: The story file states the lesson and slide 25 tells it before the logging part uses levels, files and an off switch.
place: Logging is the print statement that grew up

point: The five log levels come from PEP 282 of 4 February 2002 by Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick, in the standard library since Python 2.3.
why_critical: The story file states the lesson and slide 26 tells it before the levels of slides 27 and 28.
place: The five log levels are a 2002 design decision you inherit
